title: Joseph says they came to see “the nakedness of the land” — the Greek says “the tracks of the land”
summary: The KJV has Joseph say “to see the nakedness of the land ye are come” (42:9, 42:12). The Hebrew prints עֶרְוַת הָאָרֶץ in both verses. Brenton’s Greek prints τὰ ἴχνη τῆς χώρας / τῆς γῆς, “the tracks (footprints) of the land”.
text: KJV Genesis 42:9: “to see the nakedness of the land ye are come” Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 42:9: לִרְאֹ֛ות אֶת־עֶרְוַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ בָּאתֶֽם׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 42:9: κατανοῆσαι τὰ ἴχνη τῆς χώρας ἥκατε [to observe the tracks of the country you have come] KJV Genesis 42:12: “to see the nakedness of the land ye are come” Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 42:12: כִּֽי־עֶרְוַ֥ת הָאָ֖רֶץ בָּאתֶ֥ם לִרְאֹֽות׃ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 42:12: τὰ ἴχνη τῆς γῆς ἤλθετε ἰδεῖν [you came to see the tracks of the land] Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/GEN42.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/42/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN42.htm, https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/GEN42.htm.
reasoning: The Greek prints a different noun in both verses: “tracks” or “footprints” (ἴχνος) where the Hebrew and KJV have the word for nakedness or exposed weakness (עֶרְוָה). The accusation of spying is the same; what the brothers are said to be looking for is worded differently.
scope: T applies at Genesis 42:9 and 42:12, Septuagint only. The KJV agrees with the Hebrew. The record compares the printed nouns and does not say which is original, or that the Greek is a mistranslation. The Greek noun may be understood figuratively (places of weakness or entry); the record does not claim it is. English in square brackets is not a lexicon entry. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: The brothers plead “we are true men” — the Greek says “we are peaceable”
summary: The KJV has the brothers say “we are true men” (42:11; also 42:19, 31, 33, 34). The Hebrew prints כֵּנִים, in each place. Brenton’s Greek prints εἰρηνικοί, “peaceable”, in each place.
text: KJV Genesis 42:11: “we are true men” Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 42:11: כֵּנִ֣ים אֲנַ֔חְנוּ Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 42:11: εἰρηνικοί ἐσμεν [we are honest/right] (Hebrew); [we are peaceable] (Greek) KJV Genesis 42:34: “that ye are true men” Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 42:34: כִּ֥י כֵנִ֖ים אַתֶּ֑ם Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 42:34: ὅτι εἰρηνικοί ἐστε [that you are honest/right] (Hebrew); [that you are peaceable] (Greek) Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/GEN42.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/42/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN42.htm, https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/GEN42.htm.
reasoning: The Greek prints a different adjective from the Hebrew. “True men” or honest men speaks to whether the brothers’ account is truthful. “Peaceable” speaks to whether they come as a hostile party. In the passage the charge is spying, so the claim being tested differs between the two texts.
scope: T applies at Genesis 42:11 and 42:34 (the same pair of words also stands at 42:19, 42:31 and 42:33), Septuagint only. The KJV agrees with the Hebrew. The record does not say which adjective is original, that the Greek misreads the Hebrew, or that the two claims exclude one another; a man can be both honest and peaceable. Other Genesis uses of the Hebrew word were not examined. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: The brothers say their father is well — the Greek adds Joseph’s reply, “Blessed be that man by God”
summary: In the KJV the brothers answer that their father is in good health and bow down (43:28). The Hebrew prints no spoken reply from Joseph there. Brenton’s Greek adds “And he said, Blessed be that man by God” (καὶ εἶπεν, εὐλογημένος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος τῷ Θεῷ) before they bow.
text: KJV Genesis 43:28: “Thy servant our father is in good health, he is yet alive.” Hebrew (WLC) Genesis 43:28: וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ שָׁלֹ֛ום לְעַבְדְּךָ֥ לְאָבִ֖ינוּ עֹודֶ֣נּוּ חָ֑י Septuagint (Brenton Greek) Genesis 43:28: Οἱ δὲ εἶπαν, ὑγιαίνει ὁ παῖς σου ὁ πατὴρ ἡμῶν, ἔτι ζῇ. Καὶ εἶπεν, εὐλογημένος ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος τῷ Θεῷ [and they said, your servant our father is well, he is still alive. And he said, blessed be that man by God] (Greek) Fetched from https://ebible.org/eng-kjv/GEN43.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/43/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN43.htm, https://ebible.org/eng-Brenton/GEN43.htm.
reasoning: The Greek has a spoken line that the Hebrew and the KJV do not have. The KJV’s neighbouring verses (43:27, 43:29) record Joseph’s questions and later words but no statement about the father’s blessing.
scope: T applies at Genesis 43:28, Septuagint only. The KJV agrees with the Hebrew. The record states that the Greek has one more spoken sentence and does not say who is “that man” beyond the Greek’s own words, which text is original, or what Joseph felt. Brenton’s Greek of 43:27–29 was read beside the KJV; no other difference of that kind was found there. The Hebrew verse as printed carries a written/read (ketiv/qere) note on the verb “bowed”; that note is background and not the finding. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined.
